project_scope.note: Central Texas Ruellia-first ANATOMY teaching expanded with real physically installed examples from Ruellia, Dianthera, Anisacanthus, Dicliptera and Justicia. Retinacula/seed-count micros remain honestly unavailable; never count remote links as installed.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: First see opposite exstipulate SIMPLE leaves, then a typical Acanthaceae tubular to funnel-shaped corolla (often FIVE lobes) with 2 or 4 stamens. The highest-value confirmation is the FRUIT: commonly a two-valved, two-locular CAPSULE with seeds supported by woody curved RETINACULA/JACULATORS. This seed-support design is common but not universal; flower shapes vary greatly across the family.
family_diagnostics.leaves: Usually opposite and simple, without stipules.
family_diagnostics.flowers: Flowers often have a fused corolla TUBE and irregular/bilateral symmetry (though Ruellia can be nearly radially symmetric), generally five corolla lobes and typically two or four stamens. A Ruellia flower's large lobes differ from Anisacanthus's narrow tubular corolla or the more irregular Dianthera/Justicia flower.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Many Acanthaceae have a dry, loculicidal two-valved CAPSULE (usually two ovary locules). In Ruellia the seed is supported by a curved RETINACULUM/JACULATOR that can help eject it as the mature fruit dehisces; the structure is not universal across every subfamily.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Start with paired, opposite simple leaves, flowers, and the seed-bearing CAPSULE when available. Learn the terms CALYX (outer five sepals), COROLLA (united petals), AXIL (leaf-stem angle), GLANDULAR hairs (tip with gland) and RETINACULUM (internal seed hook). Do NOT mistake a single purple petunia-like flower for proof of this family.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: funnel corolla and opposite leaves → axillary flowering and pubescence → white and red family-flower diversity → floral bracts → external synonym example → mature capsule with two valves → retinacula/jaculators → Lamiaceae nutlet contrast
visual_lesson.intro: Ruellia is a brilliant Acanthaceae teacher: the flower is recognizable, the leaves arrive in opposite pairs, and the fruit has a remarkable (often explosive) seed-launch mechanism. Learn the easily photographed flower parts first, then examine an OPENED capsule to find the seed-support hooks. Photographs shown are species-labeled: a flower portrait is never falsely described as a capsule dissection.

steps.title: 1 · Begin with the wild petunia corolla
steps.photo_role: corolla funnel and opposite leaf shape
steps.look_for: Observe five outer COROLLA LOBES with a fused tubular throat on hairy prairie petunia. Opposite leaves help route to Acanthaceae, but mint, verbena and other families share both traits.
steps.why_it_matters: Real Ruellia flower view gives a memorable local recognition example, not a unique family proof.

steps.title: 2 · Find the flower's leaf axil and hairs
steps.photo_role: leaf margin hairs and inflorescence context
steps.look_for: Find where the leaf meets the stem (AXIL); in R. humilis flowers sit near that point rather than raised in a large branching terminal cyme. The conspicuous leaf-edge HAIRS (CILIA) help with species ID. Do not label individual hairs without reviewing exact pixel visibility.
steps.why_it_matters: Connects botanical AXIL/CILIATE vocabulary to one source-anchored flowering plant.

steps.title: 3 · Compare another axillary wild petunia
steps.photo_role: short pubescence and five-lobed tubular bloom
steps.look_for: Compare R. drummondiana's purple flower and opposite leaves to R. humilis. A useful fine-scale species distinction is SHORT, fine pubescence versus humilis's longer hairs, but this single photograph does NOT establish capsule seed count.
steps.why_it_matters: Two species can look similar from flowers, making microscopic pubescence a valuable lesson.

steps.title: 4 · White Ruellia belongs to the same family
steps.photo_role: white funnel corolla and terminal flowering habit
steps.look_for: R. metziae often has white corollas in a raised terminal inflorescence. Identify the five corolla lobes and upper leafy shoots; the exact STALKED GLAND on its calyx still needs a close, focused photograph.
steps.why_it_matters: Acanthaceae flower COLOR varies. Position and the structure of flowers and fruit carry more evidence.

steps.title: 5 · A second flower shape: American waterwillow
steps.look_for: Find the less radially even floral form of American waterwillow (accepted in this project as Dianthera americana, pictured under its Justicia americana synonym). A flower's upper and lower sides can be unequal; it is still an Acanthaceae flower.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows the family is not defined by one symmetrical wild-petunia flower.

steps.title: 6 · A narrow tube can still be Acanthaceae
steps.look_for: Flame acanthus has slender RED tubular flowers and narrow, often opposite leaves. Contrast with Ruellia's broad funnel blossoms: tubular shape and red color cannot alone establish a family.
steps.why_it_matters: Examples from different family genera counter the 'all acanthus flowers look like petunias' misconception.

steps.title: 7 · Flower bracts: compare a foldwing
steps.photo_role: foldwing flowers and leafy bract context
steps.look_for: Dicliptera brachiata shows another Acanthaceae flower and branching pattern. In a future close-up locate its enlarged BRACTS associated with flowers; do not claim the bract pairs have been precisely labeled in the whole-plant picture.
steps.why_it_matters: Small protective BRacts can be diagnostic at genus level, but must not be confused with foliage leaves or true sepals.

steps.title: 8 · One more family variation: Gregg's tube-tongue
steps.photo_role: small tubular flower and vegetative context
steps.look_for: Gregg's tube-tongue has a further floral shape and leafy habit within Acanthaceae. Look for opposite simple leaves and flower details; fruit/anther structure remains a specialty macro gap.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows breadth across local Acanthaceae without assuming a single floral shape, leaf size or color.

steps.title: 9 · Purple terminal-flowered wild petunia (external reference)
steps.photo_role: offsite licensed flowering habit from older nudiflora identification
steps.look_for: This Commons image is hosted externally, not installed as a file in the GitHub learner. It uses historical name Ruellia nudiflora; the project treats that as a synonym of canonical R. ciliatiflora. Look for a flowering stalk raised above foliage; it is a contextual photo, not an annotated cyme-origin macro.
steps.why_it_matters: Separates stem-position learning and accepted-name synonyms from image installation/rights status.

steps.title: 10 · Open a ripe Acanthaceae capsule
steps.photo_role: two locules and two splitting capsule valves
steps.look_for: A ripe Ruellia CAPSULE should show two chambers (LOCULES) and two longitudinally splitting VALVES. Do not mistake the five-lobed green CALYX enclosing a developing fruit for the two internal chambers.
steps.why_it_matters: A dry capsule is stronger family evidence than the flower's purple color. Needs a licensed photo with opened specimen and scale.

steps.title: 11 · Find the seed-support hooks (retinacula)
steps.look_for: An opened mature Ruellia fruit reveals tiny woody or hardened curved seed-support hooks (RETINACULA, also called JACULATORS). Annotate the hooks only after a genuinely sharp interior macro and actual arrow position are verified. They occur commonly, but NOT universally, in all Acanthaceae.
steps.why_it_matters: The hook-and-seed system is the family's most memorable reproductive structure and explains the fruit-release mechanism.

steps.title: 12 · Seed launch versus mint nutlets
steps.photo_role: two-valved explosive capsule compared with four nutlets
steps.look_for: Photograph a mature Ruellia capsule before and after opening, ideally with seeds and retinacula. Pair it with a true mint calyx and four separate NUTLETS to illustrate the distinction. Do not equate 'both square stems and opposite leaves' with one family.
steps.why_it_matters: Separates Acanthaceae from frequent local Lamiaceae look-alikes using fruits rather than leaf shape alone.

comparisons.title: Acanthaceae vs Plantaginaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can have tubular bilateral flowers and capsules. Acanthaceae commonly has retinacula/jaculators; Plantaginaceae does not.

comparisons.title: Acanthaceae vs Lamiaceae
comparisons.rule: Lamiaceae commonly makes four nutlets; Acanthaceae makes a capsule.

comparisons.title: Ruellia versus Anisacanthus: Acanthaceae is not one flower shape
comparisons.rule: Ruellia corolla opens into a broad five-lobed funnel; Anisacanthus often has a comparatively slender tubular red bloom. Family diagnosis rests more on total floral and fruit structure than hue or outline.

comparisons.title: Ruellia fruit compared to Lamiaceae nutlets
comparisons.rule: Ruellia often has a two-locular two-valved capsule with woody retinacula; many mints have four dry one-seeded nutlets. Opposite leaves and tube-like flowers overlap and don't prove either family.

visual_lesson.caveat: Broad Acanthaceae includes unequal corollas and some species lacking retinacula; no single flower color, stem cross section, seed hook or symmetry applies universally. Existing exact-species photos illustrate flower/foliage recognition and are NOT proof of photographed micros; three captioned steps are explicitly unphotographed. R. ciliatiflora is a licensed but linked-only external source, no physical photo installed.

previous_steps_20261009.title: 2 · Wait for the capsule
previous_steps_20261009.look_for: A dry capsule divided into two chambers.
previous_steps_20261009.why_it_matters: Fruit architecture is stronger than flower color.

previous_steps_20261009.title: 3 · Find the retinacula

previous_steps_20261009.title: 4 · Watch the mature capsule open
previous_steps_20261009.look_for: A mature capsule opening along its valves and releasing seeds.
previous_steps_20261009.why_it_matters: Links the capsule structure to its dispersal function.

family_confusion_polish.look_here_first: For local Ruellia/Dyschoriste, split a mature dry capsule to inspect seed-support retinacula; confirm two chambers and opposite exstipulate leaves. Flower color and opposite leaves alone are weak evidence.

genus_routing.Ruellia: showy tubular flower; inspect mature capsule and retinacula
genus_routing.Dyschoriste: narrow foliage and smaller tubular flowers; inspect mature capsule and calyx against Ruellia
genus_routing.Dicliptera: flower clusters enclosed by conspicuous paired bracts; inspect bracts, anthers and fruit
genus_routing.Justicia: often two fertile stamens and bilateral flowers; inspect anther structure, bracts and capsule
genus_routing.Anisacanthus: slender tubular flowers; inspect two stamens, calyx and mature fruit
genus_routing.Hygrophila: wet-site herb with opposite leaves and axillary flowers; inspect flower and capsule rather than habitat alone

confusable_families.separator: Both may have bilabiate flowers and capsules. Many local Acanthaceae show woody seed-support retinacula in opened capsules; Plantaginaceae lacks these. Retinacula are not universal in all Acanthaceae.
Usually four one-seeded nutlets and a gynobasic style in Lamiaceae, versus a two-chambered capsule in many Acanthaceae.
Opposite leaves and tubular flowers overlap; check style, mature fruit and seed attachments, not flower color.

exceptions: Retinacula are common, not universal, across Acanthaceae.
Two versus four fertile stamens is useful within genera, not a reliable family-wide separator.
Source-pool Ruellia nudiflora and R. occidentalis concepts are represented under canonical R. ciliatiflora; preserve existing aliases and native-range states.
